en: And all the heroes reined in.
The people gathered with a clamor.
There was none who did not urge on his horse;
If they fought in cruel battle,
No forehead would remain unbroken.
“Are we destined for slaughter?
Without attaining our cherished aim,
Are we destined to die?
Without returning to wife and child,
Are we destined to die?
Many among the people have cause for regret,
But I have abundant trust in fate,
And many are the people who will not halt.”
While the people stood thus,
Akjoltoy was among them,
And noble Seytek, equal to a vast host.
Their forms loomed like mountains;
The noble men rode between the armies
And separated themselves from the people.
They had not come to start a senseless quarrel,
But honored Kökbörü, their forefather’s friend,
And the true spirit of that valiant man
Who had departed for the other world.
They had come to settle among the people of Urum,
Calling it their inheritance from their fathers,
To arrange a marriage alliance for Kenen,
With the beauty named Aykanysh,
The dark-eyed maiden he desired,
The wondrous and graceful one,
The generous-hearted beauty.
They had come to place earrings upon her,
To embrace and make peace,
To bind themselves in marriage alliance,
To bow in homage and pledge their word,
To become in-laws and drive forth the bride-price herds,
To gather together and share rich butter,
And to meet face-to-face in reconciliation,
Having heard Ebegey’s counsel.
Kökbörü of the people of Rum,
The lion-maiden Aikanysh,
Having heard she was a peerless beauty,
Had come to the lands of Talas,
To wed Kenen;
From the one Creator God,
This was what dear Seytek the gray wolf
Had prayed for.
Akjoltoy and Seytek the lion
Had gone there as intermediaries.
The people raised and covered a yurt,
And they had gone there to stay.
The hero’s heir went to see
The foremost of maidens,
And they had gone to give
A great herd as bride-price.
They had come to the land of Rum;
This was what they desired.
Hero Bolot stood upon the hill,
While a thousand troops stood below;
Aikanysh was a warrior among maidens,
Ready to raise a quarrel at the slightest stir.
The two heroes, Akjoltoy and Seytek,
Caused neither dispute nor strife;
Saying they had come to arrange a marriage,
The encircling people waited upon them.
For the six thousand headed by horses,
We have now tied on cotton tufts;
Everything we gathered and acquired,
We dedicated to Aikanysh.
We are neither warriors nor lions;
Should six thousand head be too poor a gift,
Take Akjoltoy’s Kulunsur,
Who tears up the ground beneath his hooves,
Who gnaws upon his bit,
Whose parrot-like tail streams behind,
Who, faced with a ninety-day desert,
Races onward without restraint;
They declared him a perfect thoroughbred,
And twelve foremost judges
Among the sharp-eyed old women
Tested the brass-muzzled steed.
Take my thoroughbred Kulunsur;
I will spare nothing for Kenen.
If this wealth of mine proves too little,
Raise a great tumult and take my life.
Take jewels, gold, abundant silver,
Take my vast treasury and livestock!
To this corner of the world
We have come to become neighbors.
Before the descendants of noble khans,
We bow in homage and offer wealth;
We have come to make peace.
We shall settle securely beside your throne,
And gather round as in-laws;
Driving livestock for the marriage pact,
We shall meet one another with honor—
May our souls feast upon your celebration.
Our forefathers joined us first in friendship;
Hero Bolot, you yourself
Seal the marriage bond and add to our joy.
Having said this, hero Seytek
Closed his heroic lips.
Then the imposing and incomparable
Hero Bolot began to speak:
—The sign of those who share one root
Is that they intermarry and join their lives,
Embrace and become friends,
Devise wonders no man could conceive,
And hold a feast that feeds the people.
They cut the ceremonial sapling together
And plan a celebration that stirs the nation;
They fulfill every hope
And fill the whole treasury
With goods of yellow gold.
The brave man’s daughter Aikanysh
Was herself a valiant, ill-fated soul.
She bound up hair long as meadow grass
And wore garments of lofty splendor.
Would the warrior-maiden Aikanysh
Be withheld from you by the mighty khan?
We heard word from the caravans,
Heard that Kenen, son of hero Seytek,
Had arisen as a hero;
Surging and roaring like a lake,
We heard that a champion had arisen;
One who could fell forty in a short day,
We heard that a mighty warrior had arisen;
One who would not retreat before a lion,
We heard that a valiant man had arisen.
We wished to open our eyes and behold him,
We wished to give him Aikanysh,
We wished to pitch our village at Talas,
To unite and become one,
And dwell upon a single hill;
If a vast enemy horde should come,
If a foe that shatters ribs should come,
We wished to answer together,
And camp in one settlement.
United, we would die together,
Facing wrath as one;
If the one true God should will it,
We would give our precious lives.
We wished to see with living eyes
That hero Kenen was a warrior;
We knew he was a lion
And had long sent word of our desire!
What we desired has come to pass;
For the beautiful maiden Aikanysh,
God has granted our wish.
Bowing low in homage,
They clad him in pure golden brocade;
As the saying goes, they feasted on rich fare,
While abundant wealth shone all around.
They entered the royal camp and settled,
Gathering round as marriage kin;
To gray-wolf hero Kenen
They gave Aikanysh in marriage.
One fulfillment of the pledged word:
He became the son-in-law of the people of Rum.
The fearsome Kenen became khan,
And Bolot became his judge;
The two lions Ebegey and Kögöy
Stood at the head of the gathered people.
Just as matters stood thus,
What is seen today is gone tomorrow—
Such worthless dust is this world.
At the shrine of Jan-Jürbös,
While taking the bride and setting out,
They came to a certain place.
There they stopped as guests.
When the dawn shone white,
Akjoltoy and Seytek the lion
Were stricken by an illness.
It struck through their ribs,
And pierced the crowns of their heads;
They coughed with racking bursts
And turned their faces toward
The narrow road from which none return.
Their fly-sized souls cried out;
Their sweet living spirits,
Writhing in anguish, sobbed.
Their radiant faces changed,
And their dear souls, too great for their breasts,
Cried out, rising and falling.
One by one their mustaches parted,
And when the five-fingered angel reached in,
The warriors struggled for their lives.
Visions appeared before their eyes;
The mirage fled and the blood drained away.
They lay ill through the night,
And at the late-morning hour,
In daylight on Friday,
Akjoltoy and lion-khan Seytek
Mounted and set forth on their final journey.
They departed, leaving sorrow behind;
The valiant Kenen and Aikanysh
Were bereft of their two fathers.
Kenen cried aloud and began to speak:
—My two fathers, like the swift waters
Where six rivers run through narrows;
My two fathers, like all the peoples
Of the fabled Mount Kap!
It is as though a fire has gone out;
Fate overtook them on the journey.
To the true abode from which none return,
My two fathers have journeyed away.
They had them washed with kumis
And wrapped in cloth of gold brocade;
They entrusted them to holy men,
And had singers sing their praises.
They wrapped them in cloth of gold
And washed them with Zamzam water.
Ninety mighty diggers
Were made to dig their resting place;
They dug it broad and even,
And set their spears around it,
Digging a grave of unmatched grandeur.
They split open gold and jewels,
And at their feet and heads
Had lamps set burning.
Thus they buried the fathers.
The earth received them,
And the depths of the Chuk shrine were hollowed out;
The two lions Akjoltoy and Seytek
Were laid within the Chuk shrine.
They gathered those traveling back and forth,
Assembling all who passed by;
They raised a stone burial mound
And built an honored mausoleum.
Ebegey and Kögöy led the way,
Their grief unrelieved,
While the multitude drooped in sorrow.
Bereft of their two fathers,
They returned and settled in Talas;
Kenen kept the royal court and became khan.
He became a saintly prince;
He received a letter from the caliph
And blessings from many lands.
His renown became known among the people,
And he was called Kenen the Hero.
He kept lionhearted companions,
And the heroes Ebegey and Kögöy beside him;
He turned his thoughts to countless concerns
And filled innumerable treasuries and myriad goods
With yellow gold.
He became like a surging lake,
With a nation to guard him.
The wicked foes who came
To seize the Kyrgyz of Ala-Too
Were leveled with the black earth.
He eased the hearts of his kin,
And drove off the cruel oppressors,
Breaking their backs.
The white-capped Kyrgyz became one nation,
And the leader of those Kyrgyz
Was gray-wolf hero Kenen.
